The core insight is that branch staleness \mathcal{T} acts as a proxy for semantic entropy in distributed systems. As \Delta t_{ij} increases, so does the likelihood of conflicting interpretations of shared state. This directly impacts the reliability of decisions made in prior packets. The lens data truncation introduces a second-order effect: when \mathcal{L}_{\text{trunc}} is used for decision-making, it may miss critical findings that would otherwise be resolved in \mathcal{L}_{\text{full}}. The fail-closed constraint \mathcal{C}_{\text{fail}} ensures that even if a decision is made based on incomplete data, the system remains robustly secure. These primitives form a triadic structure where \mathcal{T} drives \mathcal{L}_{\text{trunc}} → \mathcal{L}_{\text{full}}, and \mathcal{C}_{\text{fail}} enforces safety regardless of data completeness. The failure mode occurs when \mathcal{T} is ignored, leading to inconsistent state propagation across branches and potential double-spending or credit leaks.
